email.body:
DevTools Weekly — Issue #142
Monday 7 September 2026

Hi there,

This week: what actually landed in Postgres 17, a short piece on connection pooling,
and two reader questions. Plain text as always — reply to this email if you want a
topic covered, the editors read every reply.

1. INCREMENTAL BACKUP, FOR REAL THIS TIME

The headline feature is incremental backup in the base-backup tooling. Previously the
choice was a full physical copy or a third-party tool that tracked changed blocks
itself. Now the server keeps a summary of modified blocks per WAL range and the
backup tool asks for only those. In our test cluster — 380 GB, a fairly write-heavy
OLTP shape — a nightly incremental came out at 9 to 14 GB against a 380 GB full, and
restore time went up by about four minutes because the restore has to replay the
chain. That trade is worth it below roughly a weekly full-backup cadence and stops
being worth it above it, which is roughly where the folklore already sat.

One caveat worth knowing before you rely on it: the summariser is a separate process
and it has to be enabled before the full backup you intend to build on, not after.
Turn it on, take a fresh full, then start taking incrementals. There is no way to
reconstruct summaries for WAL that has already been recycled.

2. CONNECTION POOLING, AND WHY YOUR P99 IS THE POOL

We keep seeing the same shape in reader-submitted flame graphs: a service whose p50 is
fine and whose p99 is four times the p50, with the difference sitting entirely in
time spent waiting to acquire a connection. Two rules of thumb that have held up for
us. First, pool size should be derived from the database's capacity, not from the
number of application instances — three instances each holding twenty connections is
sixty connections whether or not the database can serve sixty. Second, a pool that
blocks is easier to reason about than a pool that grows: blocking gives you a queue
you can measure, growing gives you a database that falls over at an unpredictable
moment. Instrument the wait time, not just the query time. If you only measure query
duration you will conclude the database is slow when in fact your application is
queueing in front of it.

3. READER QUESTIONS

"Should we run the summariser on a replica?" You can, and it moves the CPU cost off
the primary, but the replica has to be caught up or your incrementals lag reality.
We run it on the primary and have not found the overhead measurable.

"Is logical replication ready to replace our ETL?" For change capture, mostly yes.
For bulk historical loads, no — the initial sync is still the slow part and you will
want to seed from a snapshot.

That is all for this week. Issue #143 looks at query plan regressions after a major
version upgrade, and what to capture before you upgrade so you can prove one.

— The DevTools Weekly team
